You don't have any Lincoln International materials (posting, prior rounds, or notes) on file yet. The one step that starts a complete prep is: paste the job description or the interview invite (who you meet, date/time, format). I'll work from that; default now is to prep for technicals + fit for an M&A/valuation analyst.

Prep for the final round — exactly what to expect, how to answer, plus drills
1) What they’ll ask (top types)
- Technical accounting and modeling: walk-throughs of the three financial statements, working capital moves, depreciation, EBITDA → free cash flow adjustments, simple LBO building blocks.
- Valuation: DCF steps and key assumptions, comps vs. precedent logic, sensitivity tables, terminal value reasoning.
- Deal sense / transaction questions: mechanics of a deal process, your role on models/memos, accretion/dilution basics, earnouts.
- Behavioral / fit: “Tell me about yourself,” teamwork, leading through ambiguity, a time you made a mistake and what you changed, why Lincoln.
- Case or live modeling task: short case, interpret outputs or build a small pro forma on the spot.

2) Short scripts you can practice now (use your real facts to fill [brackets])
- Tell me about yourself (45–60s)
Start: one-line background: “I’m [Name]; I studied [degree] at [school] and have [X months/years] experience in [investment banking/valuation/private equity/corporate finance].” Then two strengths with examples: “I focus on rigorous, auditable models — at [firm], I rebuilt a working-cap model that reduced review issues and shaved [time saved or %] off validation — and clear client materials: I drafted transaction memos used in partner calls.” Close: tie to Lincoln: “I want to bring that model+communication mix to Lincoln’s mid‑market M&A practice because [specific reason tied to firm/posting].”
- Team win (STAR, 45–60s)
Situation: “[Deal/project], tight timeline, messy data.” Task: “I needed to produce a forecast and sensitivity for a partner call.” Action: “I prioritized high‑impact inputs, built a compact driver model, reconciled to accounting and automated the sensitivity table.” Result: number: “Delivered in 24 hours; the model changed a key revenue assumption, moving the deal to diligence — partner credited the model; we avoided a valuation swing of [X% or $Y].”
- Hard problem / technical challenge (45–60s)
Situation: “[Project with a technical gap].” Task: “Resolve accounting mismatch or build a new analysis under time pressure.” Action: “Mapped inputs to accounts, fixed linkages, documented assumptions and created a reconciliation tab so reviewers could trace every line.” Result: “Cut model errors by [X%] and enabled the team to present a clean forecast on schedule.”

- Failure + learning (45–60s)
Situation: “I missed/overlooked [issue].” Action: “Owned it, reran outputs, alerted stakeholders, and created a checklist to prevent recurrence.” Result/learning: “We recovered; the checklist reduced repeats and shortened review time.”
3) Technical question drills — answer out loud, timed

Accounting (do each in 30–45s)
- Define working capital. If AR increases, what happens to cash and why?
- How do you get from EBITDA to free cash flow? Name the main adjustments.

Valuation (45–60s each)
- Walk through a DCF’s steps and explain how you choose a terminal growth rate.
- When would you use comps vs. DCF vs. precedent transactions? Name one pitfall for each.

Deal math (30–45s)
- Explain basic accretion/dilution: how issuing shares to fund an acquisition affects EPS.
- What’s an earnout and why include one in a deal?
4) How to handle a live case or on‑the‑spot modeling
- Clarify the deliverable and time limit immediately. Restate assumptions aloud.
- Prioritize: build a simple pro forma (revenue drivers, margins, capex, working capital) and one sensitivity (e.g., revenue growth) rather than a full model.
- Keep it auditable: show your assumptions tab, use round numbers, label rows clearly.
- End with the conclusion and one risk or sensitivity that would change the recommendation.

5) Two questions to ask them (sharp, short)
- “How is modeling responsibility split between analysts and associates on a live deal?”
- “What do successful first‑year analysts at Lincoln do that sets them apart?”
6) Logistics & interview behaviours
- Confirm interviewer names/titles, time zone and link; have resume and any models ready in PDF + Excel.
- If it’s virtual: test audio/video and screen share 15–30 minutes before.
- Speak clearly, structure answers (one‑line context → action → outcome with a number → short lesson).
- If you don’t know an exact technical answer, say your reasoning step-by-step and what you’d check; don’t bluff.
7) 20‑minute practical drill to do now (self-run)
- 0–3 min: One‑line “tell me about yourself” out loud.
- 3–10 min: Pick one technical accounting Q (above) and answer aloud, then check a written model or notes.
- 10–17 min: Run a behavioral STAR for the team win and the failure; time each to 60s.
- 17–20 min: Draft the two questions you’ll ask them and confirm the setup checklist.

One next step
Paste the job description or the interview invite (who you meet, time, format) now and I’ll tailor your 60‑second “tell me about yourself,” pick the three best stories from your background, and give 5 exact lines to use in the live case. Is that the posting or invite you can paste?
